title: Climate Talks End With No Deal After Two Long Weeks
summary: Climate talks collapsed on Sunday in Antalya, Turkey. After more than two weeks of meetings, the COP31 conference ended with no deal at all. It was the longest United Nations climate summit ever held. Nearly 200 countries sent representatives, along with scientists and businesses. Each year, the UN Climate Change Conference brings countries together to agree on steps to slow global warming. It is the main way nations work together on climate action. This time, that work stalled. The talks ran far past Friday's deadline. Still, no agreement came. The European Union and other countries rejected a draft plan put forward by Turkey and Australia. Their problem? The plan did not mention fossil fuels at all. Scientists agree that fossil fuels drive global warming, and the EU said it would not back a deal that leaves out the main cause of the problem. Turkey's COP31 president, Murat Kurum, said there would be no new text. He said the 196 countries would make the decision, and he would respect it. With no deal, there will be no new help for countries hit hardest by climate disasters. There will also be no fresh steps to keep warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius, the target set by the 2015 Paris Agreement. Experts expect the world to pass that mark. Oil-producing nations such as Saudi Arabia reportedly pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the deal. Instead, they backed carbon capture and storage, a technology that traps carbon from the air. Russia also opposed mentioning fossil fuels. Environmentalists worry that leaning on that technology could keep the world hooked on fossil fuels. Experts say it is important, but it cannot fix global warming on its own. It is the first time UN climate talks have failed since 2009, when the conference met in Copenhagen.
why_it_matters: Whether countries agree on climate action decides how fast the world cuts the pollution that drives global warming, and whether countries hit hardest by climate disasters get help.

background_read: Each year, almost every country in the world sends people to a big United Nations meeting about climate change, called COP.
At the meeting, countries try to agree on shared steps to slow global warming, such as cutting pollution and helping countries hit by floods, droughts, and other disasters.
The talks can run for two weeks, and a deal needs broad agreement among the countries, so one big disagreement can stop the whole deal.
Fossil fuels — coal, oil, and gas — are at the center of the debate, because burning them is the main cause of global warming, and some countries earn a lot of money from selling them.
